questions.html:
Suppose we have a relation $R(A, B)$ with one tuple, both of whose components are NULL:

The result of:
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 11)

Answer: B. (NULL,0)

GROUP BY forms groups based on values of A. the tuple will form a group with A = NULL.

COUNT(B) does not count NULL values. Since B is NULL in the only tuple, it will not be counted. COUNT(B) = 0.

 

 

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

COUNT(*) returns the number of items in a group, including NULL values and duplicates.

COUNT(expression) evaluates expression for each row in a group and returns the number of nonnull values.


In SQL, what's the difference between count(column) and count(*)? - Stack Overflow

questions.html:
A relational database contains two tables student and department in which student table has columns roll_no, name and dept_id and department table has columns dept_id and dept_name. The following insert statements were executed successfully to populate the empty tables:

Insert into department values (1, 'Mathematics')
Insert into department values (2, 'Physics')
Insert into student values (l, 'Navin', 1)
Insert into student values (2, 'Mukesh', 2)
Insert into student values (3, 'Gita', 1)

How many rows and columns will be retrieved by the following SQL statement?

Select * from student, department
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Selected solution (score: 7)

"FROM Student, Department" is a cross product. So, all the combination of rows(3*2=6).

And you are selecting all the columns as well, which is 5 because of cross join.

So, option D is right.


Points to Note: 

1) FROM clause without a join is Cartesian Product

2) Natural Join in the above query would return only 3 rows and 4 columns

Consider the following relation:

$$
\overset{\text{Student}}{
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\rule{0pt}{2.4ex}\underline{\smash{\textbf{Roll\_No}}} & \textbf{Student\_Name} \\
\hline
1 & \text{Raj} \\
\hline

\hline

\end{array}
}
\qquad
\overset{\text{Performance}}{
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
\rule{0pt}{2.4ex}\underline{\smash{\textbf{Roll\_No}}} &
\underline{\smash{\textbf{Course}}} &
\textbf{Marks} \\
\hline
1 & \text{Math} & 80 \\
\hline
1 & \text{English} & 70 \\
\hline
2 & \text{Math} & 75 \\
\hline
3 & \text{English} & 80 \\
\hline
2 & \text{Physics} & 65 \\
\hline
3 & \text{Math} & 80 \\
\hline
\end{array}
}
$$

Consider the following SQL query.

SELECT S.Student_Name, Sum(P. Marks) 
FROM Student S, Performance P
WHERE S.Roll_No= P.Roll_No
GROUP BY S.STUDENT_Name

The numbers of rows that will be returned by the SQL query is_________________.
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 6)

The query calculates the total marks for each student by joining the Student and Performance tables based on the Roll_No column. The final result groups the data by Student_Name. Here’s how the query is processed:

1. Join Condition: The tables are joined using S.Roll_No = P.Roll_No, resulting in the following intermediate table:

Roll_NoStudent_NameCourseMarks
1RajMath80
1RajEnglish70
2RohitMath75
2RohitPhysics65
3RajEnglish80
3RajMath80

 

2.Grouping: Rows are grouped by Student_Name:

  • Raj: Combines marks from Roll_No 1 and 3.
  • Rohit: Combines marks from Roll_No 2.

3.Aggregate Function: The sum of marks is calculated for each student:

  • Raj: 80+70+80+80=31080 + 70 + 80 + 80 = 31080+70+80+80=310
  • Rohit: 75+65=14075 + 65 = 14075+65=140

3.Final Output: The query produces the following result:

Student_NameSUM(P.Marks)
Raj310
Rohit140

Number of Rows:

The query returns 2 rows, as there are 2 unique student names in the output (Raj and Rohit).

Common Mistake: Or say a silly one would be missing the names are same.

A relational database contains two tables Student and Performance as shown below:

$$\overset{\text{Table: student}}{\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \text{Roll_no} & \text{Student_name}\\\hline 1 & \text{Amit} \\\hline 2 & \text{Priya} \\\hline 3 & \text{Vinit} \\\hline 4 & \text{Rohan} \\\hline 5 & \text{Smita} \\\hline \end{array}} \qquad\overset{\text{Table: Performance}}{\begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline \text{Roll_no} & \text{Subject_code} & \text{Marks}\\\hline 1 & \text{A} & 86 \\\hline 1 & \text{B} & 95 \\\hline 1 & \text{C} & 90 \\\hline 2 & \text{A} & 89 \\\hline 2 & \text{C} & 92 \\\hline 3 & \text{C} & 80 \\\hline \end{array}}$$

The primary key of the Student table is Roll_no. For the performance table, the columns Roll_no. and Subject_code together form the primary key. Consider the SQL query given below:

SELECT S.Student_name, sum(P.Marks) 
FROM Student S, Performance P 
WHERE P.Marks >84 
GROUP BY S.Student_name;

The number of rows returned by the above SQL query is ________
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 10)

Answer is $\boxed 5$

"FROM clause without a join condition is a Cartesian Product"

You will get all the possible combination except the tuple (3, C, 80) because of WHERE clause.

So, if you group by based on student name, you will get 5 rows

Note: If the query had been, `select s.student_name, sum(p.marks) 

                                               from student s, performance p

                                               WHERE s.roll_no = p.roll_no and p.marks > 84

                                               group by s.student_name`,

 the answer would have been 2

Consider the following two tables named Raider and Team in a relational database maintained by a Kabaddi league. The attribute ID in table Team references the primary key of the Raider table, ID.

Raider
ID NameRaidsRaidPoints 
$1$Arjun$200$$250$
$2$Ankush$190$$219$
$3$Sunil$150$$200$
$4$Reza$150$$190$
$5$Pratham$175$$220$
$6$Gopal $193$$215$

 

Team
City ID BidPoints 
Jaipur$2$$200$
Patna$3$$195$
Hyderabad$5$$175$
Jaipur$1$$250$
Patna $4$$200$
Jaipur $6$$200$


The SQL query described below is executed on this database:

SELECT *
FROM Raider, Team
WHERE Raider.ID=Team.ID AND City="Jaipur" AND
RaidPoints > 200;


The number of rows returned by this query is $\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution:
Answer: 3

Selected solution (score: 5)

so the Answer is 3 

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Here, we need to satisfy all three conditions using both of the given tables:


$1. Raider.ID = Team.ID$
$2. City = 'Jaipur'$
$3. RaidPoints > 200$


By picking the rows from the $Team$ table, with the condition City = 'Jaipur', and joining it with the $Raider$ table we can get the IDs: $1,2, and, 6$
Their corresponding RaidPoints values in the $Raider$ table are:
$2 \rightarrow 219 $
$1 \rightarrow 250 $
$6 \rightarrow 215 $


By coincidence, all three rows having the above IDs have their RaidPoints values greater than $200$, satisfying the condition \(RaidPoints > 200\).


Hence, the number of rows returned is:
\[
\boxed{3}
\]

The employee information in a company is stored in the relation

  • Employee (name, sex, salary, deptName)

Consider the following SQL query

Select deptName
    From Employee
    Where sex = ‘M’
    Group by deptName
    Having avg(salary) >
        (select avg (salary) from Employee)

It returns the names of the department in which

options.html: the average salary is more than the average salary in the company
the average salary of male employees is more than the average salary of all male employees in the company
the average salary of male employees is more than the average salary of employees in same the department
the average salary of male employees is more than the average salary in the company

The query is creating groups based on $\text{deptName}$ and taking all those $\text{deptName}$ in which avg. salary of Males is  greater than company average salary.
